question: You land on an unfamiliar website making a health claim. Which of these tell you whether to trust it?
answer: The useful checks happen off the page. Stanford researchers watched historians, students and professional fact-checkers judge websites. The fact-checkers won, and fast, by leaving the site almost at once to read what others said about it. The rest stayed on the page, studying exactly the things a site's owners control.
move: To judge a source, leave it and read what others say about it.
ask: Which website did I last trust because it looked serious?

items.verdict: Anyone can register a .org for a few pounds. Lobby groups use them too.

items.note: Clean pages, charts, not a typo anywhere.
items.verdict: A good template costs little. Looking professional is cheap to fake.

items.note: It calls itself independent and non-profit.
items.verdict: Every site describes itself kindly. That is the claim, not the check.

items.note: You search its name in a new tab.
items.verdict: Professional fact-checkers do this first. It is how they beat the historians.

items.note: Its funders, found on other sites.
items.verdict: Money shapes tone. Ask who pays, and look for the answer somewhere else.

items.note: Shared all over social media this week.
items.verdict: Shares measure feeling, not truth. A good scare travels further than a fact.

source: Wineburg and McGrew, Teachers College Record, 2019
reference: Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew, Lateral Reading and the Nature of Expertise: Reading Less and Learning More When Evaluating Digital Information, Teachers College Record 121(11), 2019
